title: Motivation: The Cause of Doing Work or the Effect?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart poses a chicken-and-egg question about student motivation during the first weeks of school: does motivation cause students to do the work of learning, or does it result from doing that work? His answer is both. He walks through how resistant students are silently interrogating Credibility, Value, Effort/Efficacy, and Belonging questions before they'll try, and describes concrete moves (tracking MGCs, mini-sermons, Woodenization, Everest Statements) aimed at answering those questions yes. But he argues the more overlooked half is that motivation also flows from the work itself: consistent lesson quality demonstrates Credibility, cumulative learning builds Value, in-the-work feedback strengthens Effort and Efficacy, and simply doing things -- like his own kids learning to swim through practice, not pep talks -- is what actually builds Belonging. He closes by tying this back to his "bell is our boss" framing: every minute between bells is meant to be filled with the actual doing of learning, since that doing is itself what produces motivation.
points: Stuart's key reframe is that the Five Key Beliefs function as both a precondition for doing work and a product of doing it -- motivation is "paradoxically" both cause and effect.
He translates each of the Five Key Beliefs into a specific silent question a resistant student is asking (about Credibility, Value, Effort/Efficacy, and Belonging) before deciding whether to engage.

His swimming example -- no amount of mini-sermonizing or MGCing convinced his kids they were swimmers, only actual in-the-water practice did -- makes a concrete, non-classroom case that Belonging is built through doing, not persuasion.

The practical upshot for the first weeks of school is to prioritize planning lessons "filled with the work of learning, from bell to bell," since the work itself generates the motivation teachers often try to talk students into.
quotes: Is motivation the CAUSE of doing the work of learning or the EFFECT? As it turns out, it's both.
Does this teacher actually care about me? Does he know what he's doing? Is his passion real? (These are Credibility questions.)
The Five Key Beliefs of student motivation aren't just a cause of doing work, they're also an effect.

When my children were younger, no amount of mini-sermonizing or MGCing could have convinced them that they were swimmers. What they needed was clear, brief instruction on basic swimming sub-skills and then immediate, in-the-water, no-opt-out practice.
It was the actual swimming that quickly changed their sense of identification with the act.
And so, paradoxically, motivation is both the cause AND the effect of doing work.
